Then, we still lived in Rose. Our daddy brought me and my sister here to Sequoyah; we went to school there for about four years. We went to school there for four years, but we were coming home. Well, when my dad worked a field, he didn’t do it small. He would plant about two or three acres for our own use. My uncles and my aunt, all of us would be helping. They were plowing 40 or 60 (yu-tli-lo-da) my late grandpa and my dad. They were planting corn to feed hogs, horses, and chickens. Then we would all help. Their grandkids, my nephews, and we would all line up for them to plow. Lay out those rows. We were planting corn. When they were ready, “The Roasterneers” they call it. We were picking field corn. I hadn’t heard that there was sweet corn, it was just field corn. That’s what we were eating, also, we made cornbread with them. When I find some, the field sweet corn, I make bread with them too.

Did you grow up the same way?

When I was growing up, we were always at the water. How do you say, Spring Creek? I know they call it something in Cherokee, I forgot. Anyway, we lived nearby there. We had land and the water went through it. When it was Saturday, we went there and spent the night by the water. There were a lot of us kinfolk all over there. Some of them fished and others were gigging all through the night. Then in the morning, they’d come back. You could just hear them talking as they walked back. If they brought back any fish or crawdads, we’d fix them right there by the water. Then we’d eat. Somebody brought beans they’d cooked before. That’s how I grew up, that’s all we did. It’s bothersome, I think now. But I’m grown, I think I’m not ever going to do that again. [laughs] When Chad was born, our son, we still didn’t go to the water.

phrases.english_text: I learned a lot from my dad about raising and killing hogs. And skinning them. That’s who I learned from. He turned it all over to me y’know, to gut it. He turned it all over to me. And shooting them. The first time, “Alright, you shoot it!” he told me. I shot it 17 times. [laughs] The hog was still walking around. It was screaming. “Give it [the gun] here!” he told me. I was probably about 14 years old. I was a little scared to shoot it, but I didn’t mind skinning them. But then he told me to shoot it. He gave something to think about. I also learned to fry hog from my dad. And then my late mother, she’d say, “Alright, you boys!” she’d call us. “You all need to be learning to cook! It might happen. You’ll marry one and might not know how to cook. And when you all have children. If your wife is sick, who’s going to feed them?” That’s what our mom would tell us. “Don’t bring them here,” she’d tell us. I don’t know. But I really do appreciate it now. And I try to live the way I grew up. Like, hominy with squirrel meat mixed in. I learned that from my grandparents. My grandmother’s birthday was in November. She didn’t speak English. But when it was October, she would say, “I hungry squirrel!” That’s what she’d tell us boys. “Y’all go hunt it!” We would kill about 50 or 60 squirrels. We would skin them and Grandpa would put them in the stove to dry them. Then in November there’d be squirrels hanging all over the kitchen! Then in November, they’d get those cast-iron pots, about four of them, they’d build a fire, then they had water boiling. They had hominy cooking and they put the squirrels in with it. And I try to live the way I grew up. Like, hominy with squirrel meat mixed in. I learned that from my grandparents. My grandmother’s birthday was in November. She didn’t speak English. But when it was October, she would say, “I hungry squirrel!” That’s what she’d tell us boys. “Y’all go hunt it!” We would kill about 50 or 60 squirrels. We would skin them and Grandpa would put them in the stove to dry them. Then in November there’d be squirrels hanging all over the kitchen! Then in November, they’d get those cast-iron pots, about four of them, they’d build a fire, then they had water boiling. They had hominy cooking and they put the squirrels in with it. We’d be sitting there taking the meat off of the bones, then they’d throw it in the hominy. That was when you’d get full.
I guess they were eating good!
That’s when I got really full.

phrases.english_text: When we would go hunt and would kill a rabbit, we would step on its head and we’d pull it. Skinning it. When we went hunting, it wasn’t just us, there were about 13 or 14 of us. We’d be in a line. Then the dogs would be chasing. Then when somebody would shoot their shotgun, we would say, “Ka!” My late brother, the .44 he was going with was too heavy. I went down the hill. The dogs chased a rabbit. “Where’d it go?” I thought. I was wearing a leather cap. When I raised up over the bank, the rabbit ran by and I heard the gun go off. [garble] it said. There were bb’s stuck in it. I almost dug a hole. My brother ran to me and was barely breathing. “You’re alright, you’re alright, you’re alright,” he was saying to me. I really scared him. It also scared me. We just ate things from the woods, we didn’t have any money to get to town. I raised hogs, they were really big, but we didn’t kill them. The fat weighed 250lbs or 400lbs, 450lbs. It was this [gestures] thick.

They were making lard out of it. And then we made cracklings. We would take the cracklings for lunch at Briggs. We had biscuits and cracklings. If we had meat, we took that too. Then the white people would bring bologna sandwiches with white bread and we’d think, “Ooh! That looks good to eat!” We would go hide and eat our biscuits. We’d eat them without them being warm. phrases.phonetic_text: ayvt tsinhuhstowu skwha tsanhiwho skiwutv etot hena yotsilha'e kehv otsikvhaluhskv na'tv tantawon
phrases.phonetic_broad: ayvt tsinustowu skwa tsaniwo skiwutv etot ena yotsilae kev otsikvaluskv natv tantawon
phrases.english_text: Me, I just like it the way it was. My dad, when we killed one, we’d cut up the tenderloin. He’d cut it up into chunks and the fat. There was a cast-iron pot there. He’d build a fire and fill the pot with water and throw the meat in it. Then he’d put the lard in there. When the water evaporated then it would start cooking. He would put it high—or make it real hot, the water. When it started cooking then he would take the coals out and it did slow-cooking. When it got done, Mom would go with a pan and dig out grease from way out of the bottom. She would make brown gravy and had biscuits.

Sometimes before I’d got out of Tahlequah, somebody that knew me would pick me up. But, I don’t know how many times I had to walk home every step of the way, no ride, and it would get dark. But that’s how it was when I grew up. It was interesting the way I grew up, but I feel good about it. She was in church, but not me. My dad was a leader (singer) at the Stomp Ground. phrases.english_text: How about now, you’re Christian. Tell me what happened when you joined the church.

Well, we had made plans to get married. “Let’s go to the revival!" she told me. It’s at the Indian Baptist Church. So, I went with her, it was on a Thursday night. Really, I didn’t want to go, but I went with her. I heard the pastor preaching himself. I was thinking about when I was playing at a dancehall, instead of listening. That J.R. Stodsdill he was a missionary. We were in a big church. He was standing about 60 feet away. Boy! I was looking at him, and he looked like he was looking right at me. He was standing 60 feet away. “He’s going to come over,” I thought. Or I told him. I really don’t know. I bent my head and was hanging onto the chair. He put his arm around me. Gah lee! That really made me mad. I used to really cuss around a lot. He hugged me. I looked at him, boy, I almost cussed him out. I told him, “I ain’t ready. Get out of here!” …. [patting sound] “I’ll be praying for you,” he said. I think that was the first time I heard the gospel and about Jesus Christ dying on the cross for us. Or when a man died and He raised them [from the dead], that’s the first time I heard it. I always heard, “Quit what you’re doing.” Y’know, “Quit doing this, quit doing that,” that’s what the Christian women were saying to me. We got in our pickup and I looked at her and said, “Don’t ever ask me to go to church again.” I was all mad. Then I took her back [home.] Then, we got married in September, on the 10th… no, it was the 17th or actually it happened on the 27th in September. I was under the truck, fixing it. And she said, “Let’s go to church!” I come out from under there and it was like you had burnt my feet with fire. “Didn’t I tell you?” I said, “Don’t ever ask me that again.” “What’s going on there?” I asked. “They’re having a prayer meeting,” she said. And I said, “What is going to happen at the prayer meeting? What can happen at a prayer meeting?” So, I went with her. (Scale?) Wilson was the pastor at Cedar Tree. He preached all in Cherokee. I wasn’t listening to him, I was still thinking about the dance hall. I didn’t want to listen. Then, when he finished singing, they were doing that altar call, I was standing there, hanging on. All of a sudden, it felt like somebody stabbed me in my ribs. It was like something hit me and I was standing in the middle of the aisle. This is what I heard, “DJ, go down or get out,” it said. Boy, I was standing there looking at the door. It wasn’t no further than that door right there, I was standing. That’s when I decided to get out. I couldn’t do it. When I took a step, I just went toward where Scale was standing. I went through there and he shook my hand. “What is it?” he said. I said, “I need Jesus,” three times. He sat me down. They started shaking my hand. They were crying; the late Winn and the late Hester were both crying. “What did I do?” I thought, standing there. They were hugging me, shaking my hand. And I thought, “What did I do?” When I got up in the morning, I used to shake. My stomach, or my guts, it was just like somebody was ripping them out. That’s the way it was. Then, on the fourth day when I got up, I was going to go to work. It felt like I had lost something, so I started looking in the house. I didn’t know what it was that I had lost. I put a coffee pot on the stove, put coffee and water in it. I used to brew my coffee. Then it came to me: my stomach wasn’t hurting. I looked at my hands and I wasn’t shaking. That was when I felt like I was healed. That's how it was, which was strange to me. It was strange to me. I went to work and I was crying. That’s how it happened, that’s where it [my faith] began. But when Saturday night came, the dance hall where I used to play, I went there and I played. Then when Sunday came, I got baptized. We had a new preacher, it was diganotsah,ld, he’s the one that baptized me. Then, after he baptized me, he said, “Are you going to ask Andy if it’s all right for you to be playing round-up club?” “As long as I don’t drink, it’ll be alright,” I told him. So, I went to the club and we were playing. Boy, something slapped me. I was playing and then [slap!] After it hit, it stung. This is what I heard, “DJ, what are you doing here?” it said. I looked at the clock, it was 9:30pm. Boy, but those two hours, it felt like all night to me. I never felt that lonesome before. But I got lonesome then. Two and half hours, then we finished playing. I put up my guitar, I put it in the case. I told Buddy, “I’m quitting.” “What’s going on?” he said. “I shouldn’t be here in the first place,” I said. “I joined church.” I didn’t know how to tell him that it’d help me to let it go. So, I quit the band. I heard him telling the others, “Give him two months! He’ll be back!” they said. I preached when he died. I just about preached to the whole band members when they died. That’s how it all happened, that’s where it started. It was 1972.

Really, I didn’t want to go, but I went with her. I heard the pastor preaching himself. I was thinking about when I was playing at a dancehall, instead of listening. That J.R. Stodsdill he was a missionary. We were in a big church. He was standing about 60 feet away. Boy! I was looking at him, and he looked like he was looking right at me. He was standing 60 feet away. “He’s going to come over,” I thought. Or I told him. I really don’t know. I bent my head and was hanging onto the chair. He put his arm around me. Gah lee! That really made me mad. I used to really cuss around a lot. He hugged me. I looked at him, boy, I almost cussed him out. I told him, “I ain’t ready. Get out of here!” …. [patting sound] “I’ll be praying for you,” he said. I think that was the first time I heard the gospel and about Jesus Christ dying on the cross for us. Or when a man died and He raised them [from the dead], that’s the first time I heard it. I always heard, “Quit what you’re doing.” Y’know, “Quit doing this, quit doing that,” that’s what the Christian women were saying to me. We got in our pickup and I looked at her and said, “Don’t ever ask me to go to church again.” I was all mad. Then I took her back [home.] Then, we got married in September, on the 10th… no, it was the 17th or actually it happened on the 27th in September. I was under the truck, fixing it. And she said, “Let’s go to church!” I come out from under there and it was like you had burnt my feet with fire. “Didn’t I tell you?” I said, “Don’t ever ask me that again.” “What’s going on there?” I asked. “They’re having a prayer meeting,” she said. And I said, “What is going to happen at the prayer meeting? What can happen at a prayer meeting?” So, I went with her. (Scale?) Wilson was the pastor at Cedar Tree. He preached all in Cherokee. I wasn’t listening to him, I was still thinking about the dance hall. I didn’t want to listen. Then, when he finished singing, they were doing that altar call, I was standing there, hanging on. All of a sudden, it felt like somebody stabbed me in my ribs. It was like something hit me and I was standing in the middle of the aisle. This is what I heard, “DJ, go down or get out,” it said. Boy, I was standing there looking at the door. It wasn’t no further than that door right there, I was standing. That’s when I decided to get out. I couldn’t do it. When I took a step, I just went toward where Scale was standing. I went through there and he shook my hand. “What is it?” he said. I said, “I need Jesus,” three times. He sat me down. They started shaking my hand. They were crying; the late Winn and the late Hester were both crying. “What did I do?” I thought, standing there. They were hugging me, shaking my hand. And I thought, “What did I do?” When I got up in the morning, I used to shake. My stomach, or my guts, it was just like somebody was ripping them out. That’s the way it was. Then, on the fourth day when I got up, I was going to go to work. It felt like I had lost something, so I started looking in the house. I didn’t know what it was that I had lost. I put a coffee pot on the stove, put coffee and water in it. I used to brew my coffee. Then it came to me: my stomach wasn’t hurting. I looked at my hands and I wasn’t shaking. That was when I felt like I was healed. That's how it was, which was strange to me. It was strange to me. I went to work and I was crying. That’s how it happened, that’s where it [my faith] began. But when Saturday night came, the dance hall where I used to play, I went there and I played. Then when Sunday came, I got baptized. We had a new preacher, it was diganotsah,ld, he’s the one that baptized me. Then, after he baptized me, he said, “Are you going to ask Andy if it’s all right for you to be playing round-up club?” “As long as I don’t drink, it’ll be alright,” I told him. So, I went to the club and we were playing. Boy, something slapped me. I was playing and then [slap!] After it hit, it stung. This is what I heard, “DJ, what are you doing here?” it said. I looked at the clock, it was 9:30pm. Boy, but those two hours, it felt like all night to me. I never felt that lonesome before. But I got lonesome then. Two and half hours, then we finished playing. I put up my guitar, I put it in the case. I told Buddy, “I’m quitting.” “What’s going on?” he said. “I shouldn’t be here in the first place,” I said. “I joined church.” I didn’t know how to tell him that it’d help me to let it go. So, I quit the band. I heard him telling the others, “Give him two months! He’ll be back!” they said. I preached when he died. I just about preached to the whole band members when they died. That’s how it all happened, that’s where it started. It was 1972.

phrases.english_text: How about your preaching, when did you quit and give yourself over?

Well, 1976, that’s when I quit and gave myself over. I pastored for two and a half years at Barber. Then in Cherry Tree, I was pastor there for 12 years. Now, Elm Tree, this February will be 33 years. We have seen many fascinating things. I’ve been on a mission trip to Venezuela two times. And we went to New Mexico. We have been all over, following Jesus.

phrases.english_text: Well, when we first started, it must’ve been ’73 The Cedar Tree Four started. I helped out until ’77, then I went and pastored. I was called on to pastor, so I gave it up. The late Svdiwad started gathering up people from our association. He started the Cherokee Indian Baptist Choir. When it began, there were 40 singers. Sanders, McClemore, and all them good singers. And when JB died… Then me…

phrases.english_text: I think duck has a taste kind of like liver. If you like liver, you’ll eat duck. My niece’s husband and I cooked a duck. When he sat down, “Boy, this is good!” he said. Yesterday, we had a funeral. Last Friday, we had a funeral for a 15-year-old boy who killed himself. They buried him. And a girl came to the coffin and was there crying, I didn’t know if that was his sister. I went over there and she was crying. “What happened to him?” I asked. “He killed himself,” she said. Really, it’s going to be hard times soon. The government is wasting money. They are helping people overseas. If we get fat, he gets onto us. But here, the sick can go for help at a hospital. It’s a really good thing we’ve got going. I have really fussed about some things. These people that sit there and gripe, burns me up. I was sitting there waiting to be called. An Indian man was sitting there, but he wasn’t Cherokee, and he kept fussing around. I got mad at him. “This place is not costing you a thing!” I told him. “It is costing me!” he said. “If you are able to pay, then get out and go somewhere else!” I told him. “I think I can pay,” he said. And then when he said that he got called. There would’ve been two old men fighting, but I don’t know… Then another time, I wasn’t in church then, I was at that old hospital that was by the college. I was sitting there waiting to be called. There was a young man sitting there fussing and cussing around. “The doctors don’t know anything!” he was saying. Boy, it just burned me up! I got up and went to stand where he was sitting. “Just be quiet!” I told him. “It would be best if you just walk out and go home. Someone might get called quicker,” I told him. “If you are griping that much here. They have other doctors’ offices. Just go over there!” I told him. Ms. Carter was working in the E.R. “Tell him again, DJ!” she said [from a distance]. His face turned white. People in the hallway started clapping. I had already had my fists ready. If he got up, I probably would’ve hit him first and he probably would’ve whooped me. But he just got quiet and put his head down. Then Dr. Malabrigo called me. “Was that you who said that to him?” [he asked me.] “Yeah, it was me,” I said. [patting sound] Then he patted me on the back. But really, we don’t have anything to gripe about. They don’t charge us anything. And I get my medicine there; it doesn’t cost me anything. I see a doctor there, but it doesn’t cost me anything. When I go to the doctor, I plan on staying two or three hours.

But here, the sick can go for help at a hospital. It’s a really good thing we’ve got going. I have really fussed about some things. These people that sit there and gripe, burns me up. I was sitting there waiting to be called. An Indian man was sitting there, but he wasn’t Cherokee, and he kept fussing around. I got mad at him. “This place is not costing you a thing!” I told him. “It is costing me!” he said. “If you are able to pay, then get out and go somewhere else!” I told him. “I think I can pay,” he said. And then when he said that he got called. There would’ve been two old men fighting, but I don’t know… Then another time, I wasn’t in church then, I was at that old hospital that was by the college. I was sitting there waiting to be called. There was a young man sitting there fussing and cussing around. “The doctors don’t know anything!” he was saying. Boy, it just burned me up! I got up and went to stand where he was sitting. “Just be quiet!” I told him. “It would be best if you just walk out and go home. Someone might get called quicker,” I told him. “If you are griping that much here. They have other doctors’ offices. Just go over there!” I told him. Ms. Carter was working in the E.R. “Tell him again, DJ!” she said [from a distance]. His face turned white. People in the hallway started clapping. I had already had my fists ready. If he got up, I probably would’ve hit him first and he probably would’ve whooped me. But he just got quiet and put his head down. Then Dr. Malabrigo called me. “Was that you who said that to him?” [he asked me.] “Yeah, it was me,” I said. [patting sound] Then he patted me on the back. But really, we don’t have anything to gripe about. They don’t charge us anything. And I get my medicine there; it doesn’t cost me anything. I see a doctor there, but it doesn’t cost me anything. When I go to the doctor, I plan on staying two or three hours.
